During the 1970s, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, accompanied by half his cabinet, publicly performed acts of Islamic piety in Mecca. Clad in the simple white garments of Ihram, they were photographed kissing the Hajar-e-Aswad, the sacred Black Stone set into the corner of the Kaaba. These images, broadcast and circulated widely, projected an aura of devotion and religious humility onto the highest echelons of Pakistan's government.

Yet these displays were less a genuine nationalization of religious devotion than a hurried political submission to a rising tide. The influence of Islam emanating from neighboring Arabia had grown increasingly powerful, and Bhutto—ever the pragmatic politician—understood that aligning himself with such currents was a matter of political survival as much as personal faith. The theatre of piety in Mecca was, in this sense, a calculated gesture toward a shifting balance of power in the region.

It was in this atmosphere that the narrator's father was appointed Hajj secretary by Bhutto that year. The position elevated the family's public standing considerably, drawing them into the orbit of these religious affairs and lending them a new visibility in matters of state and faith. For a family accustomed to a more private existence, this sudden prominence was both an honor and a novelty.

The full strangeness of this new reality struck the narrator and their siblings one evening at Melody Cinema. There, amid the flickering newsreel footage that preceded the feature, they watched with astonishment as their own father appeared on the screen, dressed in the humble Ihram, mirroring Bhutto's own pilgrimage. To see him transformed into a public figure, participating in this grand national performance of devotion, was a moment of wonder and disbelief for the children.

The pilgrimage also brought its own quiet humbling, particularly for the narrator's mother. Extremely germ-phobic and accustomed to the fastidious cleanliness she maintained at home, she found herself confronted by the modest and earthy conditions of the Hajj. The crowds, the dust, and the shared spaces of the pilgrimage demanded a surrender of her usual comforts—a reminder that faith, in its truest expression, often asks the believer to set aside personal preference in favor of humility and endurance.

# The Pilgrim's Screen

I came of age in a Pakistan that was learning, almost daily, to look westward across the Arabian Sea—not toward Europe, but toward Mecca. Those were the Bhutto years, and though the man himself wore his socialism like a tailored suit, he understood the currents moving beneath the surface of the country. Saudi Arabia was ascendant then, its oil wealth radiating outward like heat, and with that wealth came a certain gravitational pull. The old syncretic faith of the subcontinent, with its saints and shrines and forgiving edges, was slowly stiffening into something more austere, more Arabian. We did not have a word for it yet, but we could feel it.

I remember it most vividly through the newsreels.

Before every film in those days, the state fed us images of piety. The lights would dim, and onto the screen would come the great white expanse of the Grand Mosque, the pilgrims circling the Kaaba like a slow human whirlpool. The camera loved these scenes. It lingered on the faces of politicians and mullahs, ministers and generals, all of them stripped of their finery and wrapped in the simple two sheets of the ihram. Here was the message, repeated week after week: even the powerful bow. Even the mighty walk barefoot upon the marble. The nation was being taught a new grammar of legitimacy, and the language was devotion.

Then, one evening, I saw my father.

Bhutto had appointed him Hajj secretary—a position of no small honor, charged with shepherding the faithful through the elaborate machinery of pilgrimage. And so there he was, blown up to enormous size, moving through the sacred sites with an expression I did not entirely recognize. My father, whom I had known chiefly as a man of files and telephones and careful political calculation, appeared on that screen transformed. He had the look of a man who had surrendered something, and I could not tell whether it was pride or merely composure.

But it was my mother who astonished me.

You must understand my mother to understand the shock of it. She was a woman at perpetual war with the invisible world of contamination. Doorknobs were her enemies; shared cups her nightmare. She moved through daily life inside an invisible fortress of handkerchiefs and hesitations, forever calculating the unseen traffic of germs. I had watched her recoil from a hundred small intimacies that other people took for granted. To touch what strangers had touched was, for her, a kind of small dying.

And yet on that screen she performed her ablutions among the multitudes, dipping her hands into the common water, pressing herself into the throng of pilgrims who had come from every corner of the earth. She drank, I am sure, from the well of Zamzam that ten thousand other lips had touched that day. There was no fortress now, no handkerchief, no hesitation. The great tide of devotion had reached even her, had washed over her particular and private fears and carried them away as if they had never been.

I sat in the darkness of that cinema and understood something about the country I was living in. This was the power of the moment—that it could reach into the most guarded chambers of a person and rearrange the furniture. It could take my father's careful pride and my mother's lifelong terror and dissolve them both in the same warm bath of belief. If it could do that to them, I thought, it could do anything to us.

The tide was rising. On the screen it looked like grace. Only later would some of us learn to read it as something else as well.

# A Journey of Faith and Reflection

There is something profoundly **humbling** about standing among millions of pilgrims in **Mecca**, where all worldly distinctions dissolve. Kings and paupers wear the same simple white garments, reminding everyone that status and power mean nothing before the divine. This experience of spiritual equality has moved countless individuals throughout history, including prominent political figures whose lives were otherwise defined by influence and authority.

The **Bhutto** family, one of the most significant political dynasties in Pakistan's history, offers a compelling example of how faith and public life intertwined in the region. Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who served as Prime Minister and President of Pakistan, and later his daughter Benazir Bhutto—the first woman to lead a Muslim-majority nation in modern times—both operated within a society where religious identity remained deeply important to national consciousness.

For leaders accustomed to command and control, the pilgrimage to Mecca represents a rare and **humbling** interruption to the ordinary exercise of power. The rituals demand submission, patience, and the acknowledgment that all human achievement is temporary. Standing before the Kaaba, even the most powerful figures are reminded of their mortality and their place within something far greater than themselves.

This tension between worldly ambition and spiritual humility runs throughout the stories of many political families. The **Bhutto** legacy, marked by both towering accomplishments and tragic losses, illustrates how public figures navigate the demands of leadership while remaining connected to deeper questions of meaning, faith, and purpose.

Ultimately, the enduring symbolism of **Mecca**—as a place where the mighty are made humble—continues to resonate across cultures and generations, offering a timeless lesson about the limits of human power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary memoir passage about growing up in 1970s Pakistan, focusing on a moment when you saw your father on a cinema screen during Bhutto's era. Use rich, complex prose.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Silver Likeness

The theater smelled of attar and cigarette smoke, of the sweat of two hundred bodies pressed into velvet seats gone bald with use. I was seven that summer, the summer the mangoes came early and rotted in the heat, the summer my mother wore her grief like a second dupatta, and my uncle—my father's youngest brother, the one who still believed in things—took me to the Regal on Nisbet Road to see what he would only call *the newsreel*.

You must understand that in those years the screen was a kind of scripture. Bhutto's voice came through it like weather, like the monsoon that would not commit itself to falling. *Roti, kapra, aur makan.* Bread, cloth, and shelter. The words had a music that made grown men weep into their collars, and I had learned to mouth them the way I mouthed the Fatiha, without comprehension but with a child's exact and terrible reverence.

The feature had not yet begun. First came the government's images, stitched together with the grandiosity of a nation still convinced of its own dawn: the steel mill at Karachi rising from nothing, the flags, the crowds that moved like a single organism through the boulevards of Lahore. And then—

I did not recognize him at first. That is the thing I have never confessed, not to my mother in her long widowhood, not to my own children who ask me now about the man whose photograph hangs in the hall. On the screen was a face made enormous, made of silver and shadow, a face turned three-quarters toward some off-frame dignitary, and it was only when he laughed—that particular collapse of the features, that helpless surrender that I knew from our own small kitchen—that my uncle's hand closed hard around mine and I understood.

*Dekho,* he whispered. *Look. There he is.*

My father had been dead four months.

How does a child hold such a thing? He was there and not there, luminous and gone, a man of light projected onto a wall in a room full of strangers, none of whom knew that the person laughing in the entourage of the great man had died of a heart that simply stopped, on an ordinary Tuesday, between the second and third cup of his morning tea. The reel did not know he was dead. The reel had been shot in some previous season, in that country of the past where he still lived, still moved, still turned to laugh at a joke I would never hear.

I have spent my life since inside that gap—the flickering interval between the living image and the buried man. This is what I want you to understand about that decade, about that country of my childhood: we lived among such projections. Bhutto himself would become one, would be reduced to a photograph, a slogan, a martyr's silhouette on the walls of the very streets where he had promised us bread. The screen gives and the screen takes; it resurrects and it lies, and it does both with the same indifferent light.

When the newsreel ended and the feature began—some romance, some brightly costumed impossibility—I kept my eyes fixed on the place where his face had been, as though by looking hard enough I might summon it back from wherever images go when the frame moves on. My uncle wept quietly beside me. The mangoes rotted in the markets. And somewhere in the machinery above and behind us, the great wheel turned, feeding my father's likeness through the light, second by second, into darkness, into memory, into the long unspooling of everything I have tried, ever since, to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in the style of literary nonfiction, the political and religious atmosphere of Pakistan under Bhutto, seen through the eyes of a child whose father was appointed Hajj secretary.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Year of the Long Prayers

I was seven years old the summer my father became the Hajj secretary, and I remember it as the year the house filled with strangers who smelled of attar and anxiety.

They came in the evenings, men in starched shalwar kameez and men in Western suits, and they sat in our drawing room drinking tea that grew cold as their voices grew warm. My father, a civil servant of the old school who believed in the neat columns of ledgers and the quiet dignity of a well-stamped form, found himself at the center of something larger than paperwork. He was to help send the faithful to Mecca, and in Bhutto's Pakistan, even the road to God ran through the government.

I did not understand then that a country could be two things at once. But I felt it in the house, the way a child feels weather.

---

There was Bhutto on the radio, his voice like a blade wrapped in silk, speaking of *roti, kapra, aur makan*—bread, clothing, shelter—the trinity of the poor. My uncle, who drove a rickshaw and had voted for him, spoke his name the way one speaks of a lover or a saint. *He gave us our voice,* he would say, and his eyes would shine. In the bazaars there were posters of the man with his sleeves rolled up, his handsome face tilted toward some socialist dawn.

But my father did not roll up his sleeves. He wore them buttoned to the wrist.

At night I heard my parents in the other room, their words traveling through the thin walls like smoke under a door. *They have declared them non-Muslims now,* my mother whispered, and my father answered with the long silence of a man who has learned that silence is a form of survival. This was 1974, though I would only understand the arithmetic later. The Ahmadis had been written out of the faith by a stroke of the parliamentary pen, and my father, whose duty was to sort the pilgrims from the pretenders, now held in his hands the terrible new mathematics of who belonged to God and who did not.

---

I remember the applicants best.

They lined up outside the office where my father sometimes took me on quiet afternoons, and they carried their whole lives in cloth bundles and cardboard folders. An old woman had sold her gold to make the journey. A man had waited thirty years. They looked at my father with a hope so naked it frightened me, because I knew, even then, that hope like that could turn to something else.

*Baba,* I asked him once, riding home in the government car, *how do you know who is a real Muslim?*

He did not answer for a long time. He watched the city go by—the mosques rising among the billboards, the slogans painted on walls, the beggars and the mullahs and the young men on motorcycles who believed the future belonged to them. Somewhere a loudspeaker crackled with the call to prayer, and somewhere else a political rally roared.

*That is not for me to know,* he said finally. *That is God's business. I only fill the forms.*

But I saw how his hands trembled, just slightly, on the leather seat. Because in that country, in that year, the forms had become God's business, and God's business had become the state's, and a man could no longer tell where the mosque ended and the ministry began.

---

The religion I knew as a child was my grandmother's religion—the smell of cardamom, the soft mumble of her tasbeeh, the stories of the Prophet that made the world seem gentle and just. But there was another religion arriving now, arriving on the radio and in the newspapers and in the tight faces of the men who came to our house. This religion did not smell of cardamom. It counted. It sorted. It divided the faithful into columns like my father's ledgers, and it decided who would drink from the well and who would thirst.

Bhutto, I would later learn, was a man of whiskey and prayer, a feudal lord who quoted Marx and a modernist who bowed to the mullahs when it served him. He had banned the drink he loved and closed the nightclubs and sent his pilgrims to Mecca, and still it was not enough. The tide he thought he was riding would rise higher than him. In a few years it would swallow him whole, and a general with a stiff mustache would hang him, and the counting would become law, and the law would become a whip.

But I did not know any of this yet. I knew only the summer of the long prayers, the strangers in the drawing room, and my father's trembling hands.

---

On the last evening I remember from that year, I found him on the veranda after the guests had gone. The Karachi heat had broken into something almost cool, and he sat alone with an unlit cigarette, looking at the darkening sky where the first stars were coming through the haze.

*Will you go to Mecca one day, Baba?* I asked him.

He smiled then, a tired, private smile.

*Insha'Allah,* he said. *If God still knows my name after all this.*

I did not understand him. I climbed into his lap and he held me, and I could hear the city breathing all around us—two million prayers and two million schemes, the sacred and the political twined together so tightly that not even a child, or a country, could ever pull them apart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an opening paragraph for a novel or memoir that blends personal family history with the political Islamization of Pakistan in the 1970s, mentioning newsreels, Mecca, and a fastidious mother.
counterfactuals.output: The year my mother stopped wearing color was the year the newsreels changed. I was too young then to understand what I watched flickering across our television in Lahore—the black-and-white processions, the men with beards like judgments, the crowds surging toward some promise I could not name—but I understood my mother, and my mother had begun to fold herself away. She had always been fastidious, a woman who ironed the creases from banknotes and arranged the spices in our kitchen by the frequency of their use, but now her precision took on the quality of prayer. She spoke more often of Mecca, of the pull she felt toward that distant stone, as though the whole country were tilting on its axis and she meant to tilt with it before she was thrown. What I remember most is not the fear, which came later, but the silence of her transformation—the way a house can be rearranged, room by room, until you wake one morning a stranger in the place you were born.

counterfactuals.output: The projector's stutter caught them first—my mother's hand, that same hand I'd watched hover over doorknobs with a tissue pressed between skin and brass, now bare and open, pressed flat against the ancient stone worn concave by ten thousand penitent palms before hers, and I felt the theater seat go rigid beneath me as the grainy black-and-white light spilled her contradiction across my face; here was the woman who scrubbed our doorbell weekly, who carried travel bottles of alcohol like rosary beads, who taught me the word *contamination* before she taught me *communion*, and yet the newsreel showed her kneeling into dust churned by countless unwashed feet, lowering her forehead—her actual forehead—to the earth, her lips moving in something I could almost lip-read as surrender, as the same mouth that once made me spit out a dropped sweet now kissed the reliquary glass fogged by strangers' breath, and I understood in that flickering silver moment that faith had asked her for the one sacrifice she'd spent her whole life refusing to give, that the God she feared had somehow outranked the germs she feared, that this pilgrimage was less about the destination than the surrender of her sterile kingdom, and I sat there in the dark among coughing strangers, watching my mother become, for ninety seconds of documentary immortality, a woman I had never met: humbled, unguarded, gloriously unclean.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a passage of elegant, allusive prose about Bhutto's turn toward Islam and Arabia, interweaving it with an intimate family memory at Melody Cinema.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Turning**

There was a season, my father used to say, when the light in Pakistan changed direction—when the sun that had once risen over Delhi and the Ganges seemed to set instead toward Mecca, and a whole people learned to orient their prayers, and their politics, westward across the desert sands.

Zulfikar Ali Bhutto—that man of paradox, schooled at Berkeley and Oxford, sipping his contradictions like fine wine—found himself, in the twilight of his power, reaching for the tasbih. The socialist who had promised *roti, kapra, aur makan* now spoke the older language of the *ummah*. He banned the drink he loved, declared Friday the day of rest, courted the sheikhs of Riyadh and Tripoli with the ardor of a convert. Some called it conviction; others, the desperate arithmetic of a drowning man counting his remaining allies. Perhaps it was both. Perhaps a nation, like a father, may turn toward faith not from certainty but from the exhaustion of every other road.

I remember Melody Cinema in those years—the great marquee blazing against the Islamabad dusk, my hand small and lost inside my grandfather's. We had come to see some film whose name I have forgotten, though I remember the red velvet seats worn thin as prayer rugs, the smell of roasted chickpeas and cigarette smoke, the collective sigh of a crowd surrendering to the dark.

My grandfather leaned close and told me, in a whisper meant for history rather than a child, that he had seen Bhutto speak once, and that the man's voice could turn a stadium into a single trembling heart. "He gave us pride," my grandfather said, "and then he gave us God, and we could never quite tell where one ended and the other began."

Outside, the muezzin's call threaded through the traffic. Inside, the projector threw its trembling dream against the wall. And I understood, without the words to hold it, that we were living in the seam between two Pakistans—the one that had danced and the one that had begun, slowly, to bow.

By the time they hanged him, the desert wind had already settled over everything. Melody Cinema still stood, but the films grew fewer, the veils more numerous, and the light kept setting, always, toward the west.

My grandfather did not live to see how far the shadow would stretch. But I have kept the memory of his hand around mine—a small warmth in a darkening theater, in a country learning, that very season, to pray in a new direction.
